body.statement: For every member of \(\mathcal M_p\), the pooled law \(P_{\mathrm{mix}}\) uniquely determines \(\theta_{\mathrm{sem}}\). After identifying \(c_0\), each nonbaseline component \(c\) has support \(S_c=\operatorname{rowsupp}(K_c-K_{c_0})\); the unique bijection satisfies \(\vartheta(c)\in S_c\), and then \(\operatorname{Pa}(j)=S_{\vartheta^{-1}(j)}\setminus\{j\}\), \(B_{j,\operatorname{Pa}(j)}^{\top}=(\Sigma_{c_0})_{\operatorname{Pa}(j),\operatorname{Pa}(j)}^{-1}(\Sigma_{c_0})_{\operatorname{Pa}(j),j}\), \(\omega_j=(\Sigma_{c_0})_{jj}-(\Sigma_{c_0})_{j,\operatorname{Pa}(j)}(\Sigma_{c_0})_{\operatorname{Pa}(j),\operatorname{Pa}(j)}^{-1}(\Sigma_{c_0})_{\operatorname{Pa}(j),j}\), and \(\tau_j=(\Sigma_{\vartheta^{-1}(j)})_{jj}\).
body.justification: The theorem identifies the baseline, targets, full DAG, coefficients, all variances, and attached mixture weights at every legal parameter point.
body.gap: Squires et al. recover a broader latent representation under their setup but their unknown-baseline Proposition 10 is false. Kumar and Sinha (2021, Theorem 3.1) identify the intervention tuples and weights in a pooled mixture of perfect interventions only when the finite discrete baseline causal Bayesian network and its observational law are given, under positivity and exclusion. Kumar et al. provide the baseline separately for causal discovery and invoke interventional faithfulness. None identifies the hidden observational component and the full centered-Gaussian SEM explanation from the unordered mixture alone.
body.consumer: Pooled perfect-intervention studies obtain a uniquely labeled structural Gaussian model without a designated control sample.
body.proof_tex:
By \(\texttt{lem:component-distinctness}\), the pooled law first determines
the unordered covariance--weight pairs.  Every finite DAG has a root:
otherwise, repeatedly following a parent in the finite vertex set would
produce a directed cycle.  Hence at least one coordinate-isolated pair
exists.  By \(\texttt{lem:coordinate-pair-characterization}\), every such
pair consists of the baseline and a root intervention, and comparison
with any third component orients the pair toward the baseline.  Thus all
possible choices identify the same input position \(c_0\).

With that position fixed, define
\[
 S_c=\operatorname{rowsupp}(K_c-K_{c_0}),
 \qquad c\in C\setminus\{c_0\}.
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:surgery-identity}\), after temporarily indexing each
nonbaseline component by its true target \(j\),
\[
 S_j=\{j\}\cup\operatorname{Pa}(j).                                \tag{8}
\]
The true assignment is therefore a perfect matching from components to
coordinates with the assigned coordinate lying in its support.

This matching is unique.  Indeed, any other such matching is a permutation
\(f:V\to V\) satisfying
\[
 f(j)\in\{j\}\cup\operatorname{Pa}(j).
\]
Choose a topological rank \(q\), strictly increasing along directed edges.
Then \(q(f(j))\le q(j)\), with strict inequality whenever \(f(j)\neq j\).
On the other hand, because \(f\) is a permutation,
\[
 \sum_{j\in V}q(f(j))=\sum_{j\in V}q(j).
\]
No summand can therefore be strict, so \(f(j)=j\) for every \(j\).  This
proves uniqueness of \(\vartheta\), and (8) then identifies
\[
 \operatorname{Pa}(j)
 =S_{\vartheta^{-1}(j)}\setminus\{j\}.                              \tag{9}
\]

For completeness, the same matching is constructive.  Among the
unmatched vertices, take a root of the induced subgraph.  Its component's
support in (8), after already matched coordinates are removed, is a
singleton.  Assign that singleton and continue.  Conversely, every
singleton choice is forced by the uniqueness argument.  Hence the
procedure terminates after \(p\) assignments.

Let \(P=\operatorname{Pa}(j)\).  Under the baseline structural equations,
\[
 X_j=B_{jP}X_P+\varepsilon_j .
\]
Acyclicity makes \(X_P\) a linear function of structural noises preceding
\(j\); diagonality and positivity of \(\Omega\) make
\(\varepsilon_j\) uncorrelated with \(X_P\).  Since the law is Gaussian,
this also gives independence, although zero covariance alone suffices for
the following normal equations:
\[
 (\Sigma_{c_0})_{Pj}
 =(\Sigma_{c_0})_{PP}B_{jP}^{\top}.
\]
Every principal submatrix of the positive-definite
\(\Sigma_{c_0}\) is invertible.  Therefore
\[
 B_{jP}^{\top}
 =(\Sigma_{c_0})_{PP}^{-1}(\Sigma_{c_0})_{Pj}.                      \tag{10}
\]
Taking the variance of
\(\varepsilon_j=X_j-B_{jP}X_P\) and substituting (10) yields the positive
Schur complement
\[
 \omega_j
 =(\Sigma_{c_0})_{jj}
  -(\Sigma_{c_0})_{jP}
   (\Sigma_{c_0})_{PP}^{-1}
   (\Sigma_{c_0})_{Pj}>0.                                         \tag{11}
\]
When \(P=\varnothing\), the inverse and products in (10)--(11) are empty,
so the coefficient vector is empty and
\(\omega_j=(\Sigma_{c_0})_{jj}\).

In the component matched to \(j\), perfect surgery sets
\(X_j\) equal to an independent centered draw of variance \(\tau_j\).
Consequently
\[
 \tau_j=(\Sigma_{\vartheta^{-1}(j)})_{jj}.                          \tag{12}
\]
Equations (9)--(12) recover \(G,B,\omega,\tau\).  The distinct-component
mixture identification already attaches each recovered \(\pi_c\) to its
covariance.  Thus the causal semantic parameter
\(\theta_{\mathrm{sem}}\) is uniquely determined by \(P_{\mathrm{mix}}\);
it has not been defined to equal an observable functional.
